title: Embodied cognitive science
summary:
Embodied cognitive science is an interdisciplinary field of research, the aim of which is to explain the mechanisms underlying intelligent behavior. It is an alternative theory to cognition that minimizes appeals to the computational theory of mind in favor of greater emphasis on how an organism's body determines how and what it thinks.

Traditional cognitive theory is based mainly around symbol manipulation, in which certain inputs are fed into a processing unit that produces an output following certain rules of syntax from which the processing unit finds semantic meaning. Embodied cognitive science differs from the traditionalist approach in that it denies the input-output system, chiefly due to the problems presented by the Homunculus argument, which concluded that semantic meaning could not be derived from symbols without some kind of inner interpretation.

The first aspect of embodied cognition examines the role of the physical body, particularly how its properties affect its ability to think. The value of the embodiment approach is perhaps best explained by Andy Clark, who makes the claim that the brain alone should not be the single focus for the scientific study of cognition. A third component of the embodied approach looks at how agents use their immediate environment in cognitive processing, as the local environment is seen as an actual extension of the body's cognitive process.

The closely related field of embodied cognition more broadly represents a diverse group of theories which investigate how cognition is shaped by the bodily state and capacities of the organism. The embodied mind thesis challenges theories such as cognitivism, computationalism, and Cartesian dualism, and is closely related to the extended mind thesis, situated cognition, and enactivism. Its intellectual roots date back to early 20th century philosophers Martin Heidegger, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, and John Dewey.
